title: I built an AI workflow that generates game worlds as reusable objects, not one-off meshes
author: SignificanceLanky988
selftext:
I've been working on a slightly different approach to AI-generated 3D for games.

Most text/image → 3D workflows ultimately give you a mesh. That's obviously useful, but for games I kept wanting the stuff *behind* the mesh too. If it's a car, I want the doors, wheels and other parts to still be separate things. I want the joints to survive. If I change something later, I want to change the same object instead of generating another version of it.

So I built a free and open-source project called Construct around that idea.

Instead of asking the model for the final geometry, the agent first researches or designs the object as named parts at real dimensions, including how they connect and move. Construct checks that representation and builds the outputs from it.

The video shows a few ways I've been testing this for games.

The [Land Cruiser](https://rtmandreyev.github.io/construct/examples/toyota-land-cruiser-fj62/) and [VW Samba](https://rtmandreyev.github.io/construct/examples/volkswagen-t1-samba/) are useful examples because they're still made from individual parts, with working joints, and can be exploded rather than being one opaque mesh. Spaceship [KESTREL](https://rtmandreyev.github.io/construct/examples/kestrel-v2/) tests the other direction: it's completely fictional, so instead of researching an existing object the agent has to [design one from a brief and real NASA engineering references](https://github.com/rtmandreyev/construct/blob/main/docs/for/invent-from-what-exists.md).

The part I've been spending the most time on recently is Worlds. Instead of generating a whole scene as one result, the agent builds the objects individually and then places those same objects together.

I tested that two ways:

[Stortorget, the Christmas market](https://rtmandreyev.github.io/construct/worlds/stortorget/construct.html), starts with one photograph of Stockholm's old square. The agent researched the actual buildings individually, reconstructed them as separate objects, and then composed the square. There's also a [walkthrough of how it was reconstructed](https://github.com/rtmandreyev/construct/tree/main/examples/worlds/stortorget).

[Rain Harbour, the cyberpunk street](https://rtmandreyev.github.io/construct/worlds/rain-harbour/construct.html), goes the opposite direction. It starts from one piece of concept art. The agent planned 21 distinct objects, built each once, placed them 50 times, checked the composed world, and exported the result as a Godot level. The full [concept image → World → Godot walkthrough is here](https://github.com/rtmandreyev/construct/tree/main/examples/worlds/rain-harbour).

[The car](https://rtmandreyev.github.io/construct/worlds/rain-harbour/constructs/auric/) in Rain Harbour still has working doors after being placed in the world, and every object can still be moved, edited or reused separately.

There are exports for glTF/OBJ, Blender and Godot, but I also added an adapter system because I don't think the built-in outputs should dictate somebody else's engine or pipeline. An adapter can translate the same underlying object into another format without changing Construct itself.

The video happens to show Construct running inside Hermes Agent, where it's available as a native plugin and the objects/worlds can live directly in the chat. But Construct isn't tied to Hermes — it can also be used as an agent skill or through MCP with other agents and clients.

It's still very much an experiment, and complex organic/curved geometry is one of the things I'm still working on. But I think there's something useful in treating AI-generated game assets as persistent structured objects rather than disposable outputs.

Repo:  
[https://github.com/rtmandreyev/construct](https://github.com/rtmandreyev/construct)

I hope some of you find it useful for your own projects. If you end up building something with it, please show me — I'd genuinely love to see what people do with it. And any feedback is welcome, especially if something breaks or doesn't behave the way you'd expect.
